tasks.task: Find a popular recipe for a chocolate chip cookie and list the ingredients and preparation steps.
tasks.answer: Popular recipe found: Best Chocolate Chip Cookies (Allrecipes, 19,331 ratings). Ingredients: - 1 cup butter, softened - 1 cup white sugar - 1 cup packed brown sugar - 2 large eggs - 2 teaspoons vanilla extract - 1 teaspoon baking soda - 2 teaspoons hot water - ½ teaspoon salt - 3 cups all-purpose flour - 2 cups semisweet chocolate chips - 1 cup chopped walnuts Preparation steps: 1. Gather your ingredients, making sure your butter is softened, and your eggs are room temperature. 2. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Beat butter, white sugar, and brown sugar together in a large bowl with an electric mixer until light and creamy, about 4 minutes. 3. Beat in eggs, one at a time, then stir in vanilla. 4. Dissolve baking soda in hot water; add to batter along with salt and mix until combined. 5. Stir in flour just until no dry streaks remain. Fold in chocolate chips and walnuts, if using, until evenly distributed. 6. Drop rounded 1 ½-tablespoon portions of dough 2 inches apart onto ungreased baking sheets, using a medium cookie scoop if desired. 7. Bake in the preheated oven until the edges are lightly browned and the centers are just set, about 10 minutes. 8. Let the cookies cool briefly on the baking sheets, then transfer them to a wire rack to cool completely. 9. Serve or store cooled cookies in an airtight container.

tasks.task: Look up the most recent papers related to 'cs.CL', select one and show its abstract.
tasks.answer: Selected paper from the most recent cs.CL papers: 'Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31646). Abstract: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.

tasks.task: Find the latest paper on 'machine learning in the Statistics section of ArXiv and provide its abstract.
tasks.answer: Latest paper on 'machine learning' in the Statistics section of ArXiv (ordered by Announcement date, newest first): Title: Phase Transition from Random Features to Fully Trainable Networks arXiv ID: 2610.31663 URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31663 Abstract: Constructing accurate and computationally tractable approximation spaces is a fundamental task in scientific computing. Partially trainable neural networks bridge fixed random features and fully adaptive representations. This paper quantifies a phase transition pattern in approximation bounds and observes analogous behavior in training errors: a rapid but smooth initial improvement followed by diminishing returns, with a sharper transition under greater initialization mismatch. Under polynomial spectral decay with exponent \alpha>1 and leverage compatibility, we establish a squared L_2 approximation rate \mathcal{O}((\kappa_P\log(m/\delta)/m)^\alpha) for two-layer networks of width m and trainable proportion P, where \kappa_P=(P/\kappa_1^*+(1-P)/\kappa_0^*)^{-1}. The bound holds uniformly over the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with probability at least 1-\delta. The constants \kappa_0^* and \kappa_1^* quantify the fixed and trainable groups' sampling mismatches relative to the target RKHS. For spherical biased-ReLU features in dimension d, we verify these assumptions with \alpha=(d+2)/(d-1) and \kappa_0^*=4\sqrt{2}\tau(d+1)/d for initialization scale \tau\ge1, and \kappa_1^*=1 under ridge leverage sampling. For d=5 and \tau=10, a trainable proportion of approximately 4.1\% captures 90\% of the reduction in the approximation bound from P=0 to P=1. A structured three-layer example illustrates how a few trainable first-layer neurons exploit fixed downstream blocks through nonlinear composition. Numerical experiments across diverse settings, including networks with up to 15 layers, exhibit similar phase transitions in training errors.

tasks.answer: Title: Fuzzy Geometries with an Internal Space Authors: John W. Barrett, Joseph Burridge (arXiv:2604.19549, submitted 21 April 2026 — the most recent result of an arXiv advanced search for 'non-commutative geometry' with author 'John', sorted by Announcement date newest first). Abstract: The product of a non-commutative matrix spectral triple with a simple two-dimensional internal space is considered. This is interpreted as a non-commutative spacetime that contains one charged Dirac fermion and its antiparticle. The inner fluctuations of a vacuum Dirac operator are calculated, using the standard technique of Connes' one-forms. This results in the non-commutative analogue of a gauge field, as expected, and also fluctuations of the spacetime geometry. In addition, the fluctuations include a derivative operator that depends on the particle charge. The integral over the fermions in the model is calculated, leading to some novel induced bosonic terms.

tasks.task: Search for the differences between "fewer" and "less" in grammar section, and provide examples illustrating their correct usage from the Cambridge Dictionary.

(https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/less-or-fewer): Difference: less and fewer are comparative quantifiers. Less is the comparative form of little and is used with uncountable nouns; fewer is the comparative form of few and is used with plural (countable) nouns. Before articles/demonstratives/possessives/pronouns, use "less of" with singular nouns and "fewer of" with plural nouns. Using less with plural countable nouns (e.g. "less pizzas") is common in informal speech but traditionally not considered correct. Examples from the article - less: "I do less work at weekends than I used to."; "It was funny to begin with, but as time went on, it became less of a joke." fewer: "Better cycle routes would mean fewer cars and fewer accidents."; "Fewer of them will be getting that information from newspapers which arrive hours after the news has occurred."; "Every year in Britain about 5,000 people die on the roads. Guidelines: indirect speech reports the content of what someone said rather than their exact words; reporting statements uses a that-clause (that often omitted informally), yes-no/alternative questions use if/whether-clauses in statement word order, wh-questions use a wh-clause without a question mark, and commands use a to-infinitive clause. tasks.task: Use Cambridge Dictionary to understand the use of articles ('a', 'an', 'the') in English Grammar, including examples of usage with both countable and uncountable nouns.
tasks.answer: Used Cambridge Dictionary to understand English articles. On https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/a-an-and-the ('A/an and the' under Grammar > Nouns, pronouns and determiners > Determiners): 'a/an' is the indefinite article and 'the' is the definite article. 'A' is used before words beginning with a consonant sound (e.g., 'a car', 'a university') and 'an' before a vowel sound (e.g., 'an apple', 'an hour'). With countable nouns, articles are used with singular forms (e.g., 'I have a sister and a brother.', 'The lion roared.'); 'the' can also be used with plurals when specific. With uncountable nouns, 'a/an' is not used (e.g., 'The rice we bought in the Thai shop is much better than the one we bought in the supermarket.'); uncountable nouns take no article when general and 'the' when specific.
